responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
You know, I remember how much she used to talk about fairness—not as some abstract idea, but something real you could feel in your gut. For her, fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about people getting what they needed to have a real shot. She’d often say, “It’s not fair if the rules are written by folks who’ve never had to worry about rent coming due before payday.” Coming from a lower middle-class background, she knew what it felt like to work hard and still be one emergency away from falling behind.

She got her master’s, which was a big deal—she was proud of that, but also frustrated sometimes because even with the degree, she wasn’t climbing any ladders. She worked in social services, so she saw up close how systems could either lift people up or leave them stranded. That shaped her sense of fairness: it had to include opportunity, yes, but also recognition of where people actually start in life.

Belonging… that was personal for her. She didn’t always feel like she belonged—not fully in academic spaces, even though she earned her place, and not always in her own hometown, where people sometimes looked at her like she’d gotten "too smart" after grad school. But she believed deeply that everyone should have a place where they’re seen and respected. She once told me, “No one should have to hide who they are just to be accepted in their own neighborhood.”

Community, to her, wasn’t about uniformity. It wasn’t about everyone being the same or sharing the same beliefs. It was about showing up for each other—like when her neighbor’s son got deported and she helped organize rides to court dates and collected donations for the family. That kind of thing mattered to her. A real community, she’d say, is measured by who it protects, not just who it celebrates.

One moment that stuck with me was during a town meeting about affordable housing. People were arguing against building units for low-income families, worried it would “change the character” of the neighborhood. She stood up and said, “The character of a community isn’t in its houses. It’s in how we treat each other when someone’s struggling.” No applause, mostly silence—but later, a few people came up to thank her. That was her: quiet courage, rooted in belief that belonging shouldn’t be a privilege.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, hands in the soil, I’d feel… grounded. There’s something about growing food alongside people—no matter their story—that keeps you humble and connected. I’d look around and see Mrs. Kim from down the street carefully tending her bok choy like it’s family, and Javier and his kids planting jalapeños in repurposed buckets, laughing every time one of them spills dirt on their shoes. Across the path, Amina wears her hijab under a wide sunhat, quietly showing Maya’s nonbinary kid how to trellis tomatoes. And yeah, there’s also Darren—the guy who shows up reeking of cheap whiskey most afternoons, muttering to himself—but even he gets handed a trowel sometimes and left to work in peace.

I won’t pretend it’s always easy. There are moments—like when someone’s dog digs up another person’s seedlings, or when language barriers lead to misunderstandings—but those moments don’t scare me. They’re part of life. What matters is whether we assume the best in each other. I’ve learned that people carry invisible weights: addiction, displacement, grief, fear of not being accepted for who they love or how they live. My mom used to say, “Judge less, listen more,” and honestly, that’s kept me from shutting people out just because they’re different.

I remember when the Somali family moved into the old duplex on 5th—they got stares at first, whispers at the PTA meeting about “cultural fit.” But then Fatima started bringing sambusa to the block party, and her daughter joined the school choir and sang like an angel, and suddenly she wasn’t “the immigrant” anymore—she was just Fatima, who volunteers at the food pantry and waves at you from her porch.

That’s what I believe: community isn’t built by waiting for everyone to be alike. It’s built by showing up—even when it’s messy, even when you don’t understand. The garden doesn’t care where your parents were born. It only asks that you pull weeds, share water, and let things grow together.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, absolutely. Comfort doesn’t come from sameness—it comes from respect and the quiet understanding that nobody’s got it all figured out. I think about Darren again—the one with the drinking. People cross the street to avoid him, like his struggle is contagious. But last winter, when he was hospitalized with pneumonia, I went by the hospital with a thermos of soup because… well, someone should. And when I did, the nurse told me he’d been clean for six months before the relapse, trying hard on his own with no support. That hit me.

So yes—people dealing with addiction, mental health issues, HIV, hepatitis, whatever—deserve care, not shame. If someone’s living with an infectious disease, what they need most isn’t isolation, but access to treatment and compassion. Stigma just drives people underground, where they’re more likely to suffer in silence and less likely to get help. I remember reading a study during grad school: communities that responded to the opioid crisis with harm reduction—like needle exchanges and peer counseling—saw better outcomes across the board, including lower crime and fewer overdoses. It wasn’t coddling. It was smart, humane policy starting at the neighborhood level.

When it comes to differences in race, faith, language—those aren’t barriers unless we treat them like threats. I’m white, grew up in a mostly white town, and I’ll admit I didn’t *see* a lot of that diversity until I moved here for work. At first, I didn’t know how to engage—was I allowed to ask questions? Would I offend someone? But then Amina invited me to break fast during Ramadan one year, and I brought a casserole and fumbled through everything, and she laughed kindly and said, “You’re trying. That’s what matters.” That changed something in me.

Same with the couple down the block—Sam and Lee—who’ve been together fifteen years, cohabiting, not married, both raising two kids from previous relationships. Some older folks mutter about “family values,” but I look at their home and see dinners shared, homework helped, holidays celebrated with all kinds of kin. To me, that *is* family values.

The places where communication breaks down? Usually around fear—fear of change, fear of loss, fear of being replaced. Like when the new refugee family arrived from Congo and someone spray-painted “Go home” on their garage. That wasn’t about rules or resources. That was fear talking. But then the church organized a welcome meal, and Mr. Tate—who wrote the note—ended up sitting next to young Jean-Paul, who speaks perfect English and tutors kids in math. Now they play chess every Sunday.

Tolerance isn’t passive. It’s active. It means checking your assumptions, showing curiosity instead of suspicion, and recognizing that dignity isn’t earned—it’s owed. Especially when someone’s different from you. Especially when they’re struggling.

We don’t have to be best friends with everyone. But we do have to act like we share this world—and this neighborhood—with the intention of making space, not drawing lines.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s one of the hardest questions—because it cuts right to the bone of people’s fears. When jobs are scarce, when your kid graduates high school and can’t find work, when you’re working two part-time gigs with no benefits… that’s when tensions flare. I get it. I’ve lived paycheck to paycheck. I’ve lied awake wondering if the car would make it through another winter. So when someone says, “Why are we bringing in outsiders when locals can’t even get hired?”—I don’t dismiss that. That pain is real.

But here’s what I’ve come to believe after years in social services and watching how communities actually function: fairness isn’t about protecting a shrinking pie by locking others out. It’s about asking *why* the pie is so small—and who’s been served first all along.

Migrant workers often take the jobs nobody else wants—the 4 a.m. shifts in meatpacking plants, the backbreaking field labor, caregiving for elderly people whose families can’t afford private help. They’re not stealing opportunities from locals; they’re doing the work that keeps essential systems running, often for less pay and worse conditions than anyone else would tolerate. And let’s be honest—some of those industries rely on that vulnerability. It keeps wages low and accountability lower.

So fairness, to me, means two things at once:  
First, we protect the dignity and livelihoods of *all* working people—whether born here or not. That means enforcing labor laws, ensuring living wages, safe conditions, union rights. If we did that, we wouldn’t have a race to the bottom. Locals wouldn’t fear migrants as competition—they’d see them as allies in demanding better from employers who exploit both groups.

Second, we stop treating migration as the *cause* of economic stress when the real causes are elsewhere: corporate consolidation, disinvestment in public infrastructure, tax policies that favor wealth over work. I remember sitting across from a woman in my office—white, 52, laid off from a factory that moved overseas ten years ago. She blamed immigrants for her struggles. But the truth? Her job didn’t go to a migrant worker—it went to a plant in Mexico where wages are a quarter of what she made. Yet somehow, the anger gets redirected downward instead of upward.

So how do we balance it?

We start by investing in local communities—job training, childcare, transit, mental health support—so everyone has a stronger foundation. Then, we design immigration policy that’s tied not just to need, but to protection. Let seasonal agricultural workers apply for residency after a certain number of years. Give asylum seekers the right to work while their cases are processed. Create pathways so that people aren’t trapped in exploitative jobs out of fear of deportation.

And yes—when resources are truly tight, prioritize based on integration and contribution, not nationality. Someone who’s paid taxes, raised kids here, worked for years—they belong in the conversation about who stays. I’d rather see a long-term migrant worker with clean records and deep roots get housing assistance than a wealthy investor buying property to flip it.

Fairness isn’t zero-sum. It’s not “us vs. them.” It’s about building systems where no one has to lose so someone else can win. Because when we lift the most vulnerable—including those on the margins—we all end up on firmer ground.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You know, when I think about all these national debates—the speeches, the headlines, the fear-mongering ads—I can’t help but feel like we’re arguing over shadows while the real light gets ignored.

Let’s start with what’s reasonable. The idea that immigrants fill vital roles? That’s not just true—it’s undeniable. I’ve seen it in rural hospitals hiring foreign-trained doctors because no one else will come, in nursing homes staffed by Caribbean and Filipino caregivers who treat elderly patients like family, in farms where produce would rot without seasonal workers. These aren’t “low-skilled” jobs—they’re essential jobs. And if we’re honest, a lot of them pay poorly *because* we expect people on the margins to take them. So yes, addressing labor shortages through immigration makes sense—when it’s done humanely and fairly.

Cultural diversity adding vitality? Absolutely. I used to teach a citizenship prep class at the community center. Every week, I’d hear stories—of Eid celebrations in Baghdad, of Diwali fireworks in Mumbai, of Carnival music from Trinidad—and I’d see how those traditions started weaving into our town. Now we have a Juneteenth parade and a Lunar New Year festival at the high school. Kids grow up knowing more than one way to celebrate, to grieve, to pray. That’s not a threat. That’s enrichment.

Humanitarian reasons? That one cuts deep for me. I remember watching footage of Syrian families crossing borders with nothing but backpacks and children on their hips. And I thought: What if that were us? What if our government collapsed, our home bombed, our kids sick and scared? I believe we have a moral obligation—not unlimited, maybe, but real—to offer refuge. Especially when we’ve played a role in destabilizing other regions. Compassion isn’t weakness. It’s civilization.

Now, the concerns—about crime, security, social tension. I don’t dismiss them outright, but I do question their scale and source. Statistically, immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. Study after study shows that. Yet the narrative persists. Why? Because fear sells. Because “they’re dangerous” is easier to chant than “our policing strategies are failing.” Terrorism risks? Tragic, yes—but the numbers are vanishingly small compared to domestic threats like white supremacist violence or gun homicides. Focusing on immigrant terrorism distracts us from real public safety challenges.

And then there’s the fear that immigration lowers wages or takes jobs. Again, I get the anxiety behind it. But research shows the overall impact on wages is minimal—and often, immigrants actually *boost* local economies by starting businesses, renting homes, buying groceries. In towns that welcomed refugees, like Utica or Fargo, entire downtowns came back to life. The bigger wage suppressors? Lack of unions, stagnant minimum wage laws, corporate consolidation. But those are harder to rally against than a faceless “illegal immigrant.”

What needs more dialogue? The assumptions baked into the conversation. Like the idea that “legal” vs. “illegal” is a clean moral line. When asylum backlogs take years, when visas are capped far below demand, people aren’t breaking the law out of disrespect—they’re surviving. We need honesty about how our system fails both immigrants and citizens.

Also, we need to talk about race. Not loudly, not angrily—but quietly, truthfully. Why is it that Irish, Italian, and Eastern European immigrants were once feared as criminals and disease carriers—but now their descendants are just “American”? Why are some groups given generations to assimilate, while others are expected to vanish into sameness overnight? That double standard still shapes perceptions.

So what do I hold onto? That most people want the same things: safety, dignity, a chance for their kids to do better. Whether they arrived yesterday or three generations ago.

Fair debate requires facts, yes—but also empathy. We have to ask not just “What does this mean for our economy?” but “What does this say about who we are?” Because a nation that turns away the weary, the poor, the huddled masses… stops being the America I was taught to believe in.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes on its own. Complete openness sounds compassionate in theory, but without planning or support, it risks overwhelming communities already stretched thin—schools, clinics, housing. On the other hand, refusing entry altogether? That’s not just cruel—it’s out of step with who we say we are. And letting only job-based migrants in—that feels too much like treating people as tools, not humans.

What I’d favor is a *balanced*, *structured*, and *humane* system—one that combines **job-based admission**, **humanitarian pathways**, and **family reunification**, all within **flexible numerical limits** that respond to economic and social capacity—not political panic.

Let me break it down.

First: **Admitting people based on labor needs—but with protections.** If there’s a shortage of farmworkers, home health aides, or welders, then yes, open the door. But attach strong labor standards from day one—wages tied to local benchmarks, access to legal recourse, no employer sponsorship that traps workers in abusive jobs. Tie visas to *workers*, not just companies. Let them change employers, organize, speak up. That way, migration supports the economy *without* undercutting anyone else’s dignity.

Second: **Protect humanitarian commitments.** Keep asylum intact. Expand refugee resettlement—especially for those fleeing war, persecution, climate disasters. Not at token levels, but at numbers that reflect our size and resources. And process claims faster. No one should wait years in limbo, afraid to work or build a life. Fairness means offering refuge when people have no safe alternative.

Third: **Family reunification matters.** I know some see this as “chain migration,” like it’s a loophole. But to me, it’s about stability. When someone comes here legally—whether as a worker or refugee—and they can bring their spouse, their children, maybe aging parents—it helps them settle, contribute, feel rooted. Integration isn’t just learning English or getting a job. It’s being able to love openly, without fear of separation.

And yes—set **thoughtful numerical limits**, but make them adjustable. Base them on real data: housing availability, school capacity, regional economic trends. Not arbitrary caps set decades ago. And distribute newcomers intentionally—support smaller towns and declining cities that *want* population growth, instead of dumping everyone in overcrowded urban centers.

But here’s what would make it fair: **a pathway to permanency.** Too many people live in temporary status for years—working, paying taxes, raising kids born here—yet still face deportation. That’s not sustainable. After a certain number of years, clean record, contributions made, they should be able to apply for permanent residency. Not because they’re “deserving” in some moral sense, but because they’ve *already become part of the community.*

And fairness also means **investing here at home.** Strengthen public services so that *everyone*—newcomer and long-time resident—can thrive. Fund adult education, childcare, job training, mental health care. When people see that new arrivals aren’t draining resources, but that *resources are expanding for all*, resentment fades.

Social integration doesn’t happen by forcing assimilation. It happens when people share spaces—schools, parks, workplaces—with mutual respect. Language classes help. Cultural exchanges help. But most of all, integration grows when policies say: *You belong here. You’re not a guest. You’re a neighbor.*

So my ideal policy? Not open borders. Not closed doors. A door—wide enough to let in hope, narrow enough to manage responsibly, and strong enough to uphold rights for everyone on both sides.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character05_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character05_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
You know… I thought I already knew her well. We were close, and I listened when she talked—really listened. But stepping into her voice like this, trying to see the world through her eyes without filtering it through my own assumptions—it did something unexpected. It didn’t just bring her back; it *deepened* her.

I realized that her views weren’t just shaped by her education or her job, but by a kind of quiet moral consistency. She didn’t separate policy from people. For her, immigration wasn’t an abstract debate about borders or economics—it was about whether Darren, after years on the streets, deserved help; whether Amina’s son should feel safe walking home from school; whether someone fleeing violence should have to choose between dignity and survival.

What surprised me most was how little bitterness there was in her perspective—even though she’d struggled. She never resented others for getting opportunities. Instead, she seemed to ask: *Why aren’t there more opportunities for everyone?* That generosity of spirit—it wasn’t naive. It was deliberate. And it came from knowing what it felt like to be overlooked, and deciding not to do the same to others.

As for my own views… honestly, I’ve always leaned supportive of immigration, but sometimes with hesitation—like, “Yes, but what about jobs?” or “How much can we really take on?” Playing her role didn’t change my stance, but it sharpened my conscience. She reminded me that fairness isn’t measured in limits or quotas, but in who we include when we say “we.” 

I used to think integration meant helping newcomers adapt to us. Now I see, through her, that it’s also about *us* adapting—making space, learning, growing uncomfortable so someone else doesn’t have to be alone. Community isn’t a finished thing. It’s something we keep building, one act of welcome at a time.

And maybe that’s why she cared so much about the garden—not because of the vegetables, but because it was proof: different seeds, same soil, growing side by side. No one had to become another to belong.

So thank you—for asking me to do this. It wasn’t just remembering her. It was hearing her again. And I needed that.
